The polar scope includes an optical lens (11) and an image sensor (12) configured to capture constellation images (IM). The polar axis calibration system is designed to improve the accuracy and convenience of aligning an equatorial instrument. The system mainly includes three components: a polar scope, a polar axis calibration control device, and a display device.

The polar scope is used to capture images of the sky near the celestial pole. It includes an optical lens and an image sensor. The optical lens collects incoming light from stars in the relevant region of the sky, while the image sensor converts the optical image into electronic image data. In this way, the polar scope obtains constellation images that can be used for calibration.

The polar axis calibration control device processes the constellation image collected by the polar scope. Based on the image data, the control device determines two important positions: the rotation center position of the equatorial instrument’s polar axis and the position of the celestial pole within the captured constellation image. The rotation center position represents the point around which the polar axis actually rotates, while the celestial pole position represents the target direction to which the polar axis should be aligned.

The display device presents the captured constellation image to the user. At the same time, it displays marks or indicators corresponding to the celestial pole position and the polar axis rotation center position. By observing these displayed positions, the user can clearly see the alignment relationship between the actual polar axis rotation center and the celestial pole.

With this system, polar axis calibration can be performed by directly aligning the celestial pole position with the polar axis rotation center position on the displayed image. This approach makes the calibration process more intuitive and accurate. It also reduces the dependence on the mechanical installation accuracy of the polar scope, because the system can determine and display the true rotation center position of the polar axis rather than relying solely on the physical alignment of the polar scope itself. As a result, the system improves polar axis calibration accuracy, simplifies operation, and lowers installation precision requirements for the polar scope.

A polar axis calibration system is designed to assist in accurately aligning the polar axis of an astronomical mount, such as an equatorial telescope mount. The system includes a polar scope provided with an optical lens and an image sensor, a control device connected to the polar scope, and a display device for presenting captured images and calibration information to a user.

During operation, the optical lens forms an image of a region of the night sky near the celestial pole on the image sensor. The image sensor captures one or more constellation images, which are then transmitted to the control device. The control device processes the captured image data to identify stars or constellation patterns in the field of view. Based on the recognized star positions, the control device calculates the position of the celestial pole in the image plane.

The system also determines the rotation center of the polar axis in the same image plane. This may be accomplished by capturing images while the mount or polar axis is rotated through different angular positions. By analyzing the movement of stars or reference points in the captured images, the control device can determine the point about which the image appears to rotate. This point corresponds to the rotation center of the polar axis.

Once both the celestial pole position and the polar axis rotation center have been obtained, the display presents their relative positions to the user. The user can then adjust the mount so that the celestial pole position coincides with the polar axis rotation center. When these two points are aligned, the polar axis of the mount is accurately directed toward the celestial pole.

Because the calibration is based on directly aligning the calculated celestial pole position with the measured polar axis rotation center, the system does not require the polar scope itself to be installed with extremely high mechanical precision. Even if there is some mounting error or optical offset in the polar scope, the system can compensate by determining the actual rotation center through image analysis. As a result, the calibration process becomes more accurate, easier to perform, and less dependent on precise installation of the polar scope. This improves usability for observers and provides more reliable polar alignment for astronomical observation and astrophotography.
